MR. WATSON  CORRECTION OF STATEMENT RESPECTING BUDGET VOTE
speechtext:
I rise on a question of personal privilege, Mr. Speaker. Yesterday afternoon, after the budget vote, you asked me whether I was in my seat at the time the motion was put. I had entered my seat as you were finishing the reading of the motion. I was confused as to the exact time when the motion is considered as having been put, and I answered your question, Mr. Speaker, in the affirmative. I felt I had the right to vote.
Afterward I learned that the rule is that a member of the house must be in his seat when the Speaker starts to read the motion being put. I was not in my seat at that time; therefore my answer to you should have been no. I wish to apologize to you, Mr. Speaker, and to the house for having given you an incorrect answer, but an answer which I believed at the time was correct. I should like to add, Mr. Speaker, that I pledge myself henceforth to learn my procedure from the rule book and not in this very embarrassing way.

maintopic: BEST WISHES TO PRIME MINISTER FOR RECOVERY FROM ILLNESS

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: BEST WISHES TO PRIME MINISTER FOR RECOVERY FROM ILLNESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if the house will allow me to rise at this moment, I wish to say I have just learned that the Prime Minister has been admitted to hospital. I want to express, not only on behalf of the opposition but I am sure on behalf of all hon. members of the house, my hope that he will soon be restored to health and returned to the house.
I know something of the tremendous load of responsibility that rests on a prime minister. I realize that had the course of parliament been otherwise for the past few days, the Prime Minister probably would have entered hospital earlier. These are some of the things that those in private life do not understand, and foremost is the sense of responsibility that rests on one who has the office of prime minister. I want to extend to him the very best of good wishes.

maintopic: BEST WISHES TO PRIME MINISTER FOR RECOVERY FROM ILLNESS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, having learned just prior to coming into the house of the illness of the Prime Minister and of his being admitted to hospital, I share the sentiments that have been expressed by the leader of the official opposition, and on behalf of the members of the Social Credit party in this house I wish to assure the right hon. Prime Minister, his government and every member of his party of our concern at his illness, and we express our best wishes and prayers for his speedy recovery.

maintopic: BEST WISHES TO PRIME MINISTER FOR RECOVERY FROM ILLNESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the members of this group join with the right hon. Leader of the Opposition, the leader of the Social Credit party, and I am sure with the government in expressing our sincere regret that the Prime Minister has found it necessary to go to hospital. I think we are all aware that had it not been for the very heavy burden he had been carrying in recent weeks, he would have gone to hospital much earlier.
I think it would be most appropriate if you, sir, were to convey on behalf of all members of all parties in this house our sincere regrets to the Prime Minister that he has found it necessary to be in hospital, and express to him our hope for a very speedy return to health and strength.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: BEST WISHES TO PRIME MINISTER FOR RECOVERY FROM ILLNESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure it would be the wish of the right hon. Prime Minister that I should rise at this time to express to the right hon. Leader of the Opposition, the leader of the Social Credit party and the leader of the New Democratic party my thanks and those of the government for the very kind words that have been expressed by those who have taken part in this appreciation of the Prime Minister.
All I can say is that the task of carrying on in his stead will fall upon my shoulders, and I hope I shall receive the co-operation not only of those who sit on this side of the house but of all hon. members, so that during the time the Prime Minister will be in hospital, because what he will see happening in the house, his recovery will be that more prompt.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON PROPOSED CHANGES IN ACT

speechtext:
Hon. J. R. Garland (Minister of National
Revenue): Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a brief statement on one or two housing matters. You will recall that in the budget brought down on June 13 my colleague the Minister of Finance referred to a lower rate of interest on National Housing Act loans, higher maximum loan amounts and larger loans in relation to lending value.
The new 6J per cent interest rate became effective, of course, on June 14. It applied to new loan applications and applications in process at the time of the amendment. The reduced rate was also made available to
C.M.H.C. borrowers where loans had been approved at the 6 A per cent interest rate and where the mortgage had not been registered. In the case of previously committed approved lenders loans, this is a matter for their discretion.

The governor in council has now approved new ceilings on N.H.A. loans. Until recently maximum N.H.A. loans were set by regulation at different levels for home ownership and rental housing. The maximums distinguish only between apartments and other types of housing. The maximum loan for any house or multiple family dwelling other than an apartment is increased to $15,600 for each unit having four or more bedrooms and to $14,900 for each unit containing less than four bedrooms, whether the dwellings are to be occupied by the owner or rented. The maximum loan for fully serviced apartment dwellings is raised to $12,000 per unit from $8,750. The increase also applies for rental loans and loans to home owners if the application for the increase is received prior to the interest adjustment date established in the mortgage document. On loans to builders the increase will be available if the application for the increase is received prior to the loan being fully advanced.
C.M.H.C. is ready to insure loans and make direct loan commitments, subject only to a provisional loan amount pending an amendment to the act. Here I refer to legislation already on the order paper and which, amongst other things, seeks authorization for N.H.A. loan ratios of 95 per cent of the first $13,000 instead of the present $12,000 of lending value. In the interval, and to avoid delays, C.M.H.C. and approved lenders have been authorized to establish loan amounts on the basis of the proposed amendment and to issue conditional commitments in the higher amounts.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON PROPOSED CHANGES IN ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the house has listened, I am sure, with some interest as far as we could hear the hon. gentleman, because of some confusion, to the details of the statement he has just made. I am sure no one realizes better than the minister himself that this is a very technical and complicated matter and certainly no one can deal with it objectively at this time, not having seen the purport of the statement he has just made to the house.
All I can say is that anything which assists in the development of the housing industry in this country, in view of the action taken recently by this government in curtailing it, will be very, very acceptable to the house generally. We will have to consider in detail the statement which has been made by the minister, and as far as the official opposition are concerned we will deal with it objectively when we have the measures before us.

Consumer Credit
minister. It seems to me that the increase in the amount of money that can be borrowed, if we continue with the 11 per cent sales tax, will mean that interest will be charged on the increased loan plus the 11 per cent, and actually the result will be that the total cost will be twice as much as it would otherwise be. In other words we are going to have an increase here far beyond what we normally would have.

I agree with the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings that this must be viewed in the light of the 11 per cent tax on building materials. However, in itself this will assist some groups. We hope the government will continue to have in mind the need of housing for income groups which cannot meet the present loan standards. This is a great deficiency which needs to be remedied in this country.

speechtext:

[Editor's note: The statement is as follows:]
On November 23, 1962, a motor vehicle registered in the name of Richard Thibault was given a ticket for illegal parking on parliament hill. Two warning tickets had been delivered to the owner of the said motor vehicle for other traffic offences on federal property. The two warnings and the last ticket were written both in French and English.
Then, an instruction was filed on December 5, 1962 with the magistrate's court in Ottawa. Summons in English, to appear on December 19 was addressed to Mr. Thibault by the clerk of the court. Mr. Thibault did not appear on December 19. The magistrate ordered that a copy of the summons be personally served to Mr. Thibault. The next day, the first summons sent to Mr. Thibault was returned by him accompanied by the following words:
"Write to me in French. I am from Quebec". The clerk of the court asked a bilingual member of his staff to telephone Mr. Thibault to explain the contents and circumstances of the summons. Mr. Thibault informed them that he would not comply with the summons, because it was not written in French.
It should .be noted that a warrant of arrest issued by the court and delivered by the municipal police of Ottawa in view of arresting Mr. Thibault, was then already in existence. I have been told that Mr. Thibault was holding seventeen unpaid tickets for having violated the traffic rules in the city of Ottawa, which tickets, of course, are not under the jurisdiction of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
On April 1, a municipal policeman of the city of Ottawa personally delivered a summons with regard to the traffic violation committed on November 23, 1962, on federal property. Mr. Thibault did not answer the summons and he was told that a warrant of arrest issued by the court was held for his arrest. Moreover, he was informed that if he appeared of his own free will, that warrant would not be carried out. He did not appear.


Subsequently, a bilingual officer of the R.C.M.P. telephoned Mr. Thibault to discuss the matter with him and offered to discuss it in French. Mr. Thibault stated that he was doing very well in English, but that he would have nothing to do with any document written in English.
On May 10, the court warrant was duly signed by Mr. J. Rochon, justice of the peace in and for the district of Hull. No step was taken to execute until June 18, 1963, and Mr. Thibault had every opportunity to change his mind.
On June 18, a bilingual officer of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police came to Mr. Thi-bault's house to execute the warrant. Mr. Thibault answered the door, he was informed of the contents of the warrant and immediately asked whether it was written in French or English. The reply was that it was written in English and the officer asked him to accompany him. Mr. Thibault closed the door in the face of the officer. Another R.C.M.P. officer who was in the area joined the first one and both tried through the door to discuss with Mr. Thibault who refused to come to the door.
Sometime later, three men came with movie projectors and a mobile unit of a local radio station appeared on the site. The officers were wondering whether they should execute the warrant for arrest, and contacted their office for instructions. They were advised to come back and not to execute the warrant at that time.
I was told that the magistrate court in Ottawa as a practice serves all local summonses in English, but that bilingual interpreters are available to give assistance to any person in need of such a service. The serving of local summons obviously comes under the jurisdiction of the Ontario government.
The facts of the case are therefore that Mr. Thibault, after two warnings, received a traffic ticket. The subsequent procedure and the serving of summons were in accordance with the procedure in the Ottawa magistrate court. At the present time there is a warrant for his arrest issued by the court for offences on federal government property. That warrant will be executed in due time. I understood that another warrant had been issued for his arrest on seventeen counts of traffic violation within the limits of the city of Ottawa.

However, Mr. Speaker, if it is the wish of hon. members I shall be glad to read the statement which I have before me now. The statement made by the Prime Minister is as follows:
I am happy to inform you that the government has developed proposals designed to maintain employment in your community. They are proposals to provide for further uranium production until next summer so that alternative sources of employment can be developed meantime.
The production of uranium has declined sharply in recent years and, under present contracts, a further sharp decline will take place in the course of this summer and next winter. The government has carefully examined the possibilities of maintaining production and employment in the uranium mining industry by means of a stockpiling program. The eventual prospects for a revival in world demand for uranium are good. But, as far as can now be foreseen, the revival will not be fast enough or large enough to justify a full stockpiling program meantime. The stocks accumulated would be of such size, in relation even to the reviving demand, that they could exert a depressing influence on the price of uranium for many years. Extended stockpiling therefore would not be in the national interest.
The government however recognizes that it has a duty to help provide a breathing space during which alternative sources of employment can be

developed in the communities affected. Past uncertainty and lack of action have created a situation in which the further adjustment these communities face cannot be made smoothly.
The government accordingly announces that strictly as a short term measure it is prepared to buy, and to stockpile, the quantities of uranium that will enable certain mines to maintain present employment until July 1, 1964 at prices which will cover the operating costs of the mines to that date. The companies concerned have been informed of this offer and the government believes that satisfactory arrangements can be negotiated with them. When this has been done, the proposal will be put before parliament for approval.
The three mines affected are Milliken and Denison mines at Elliot Lake and Faraday mine at Bancroft. These are the mines which could continue to operate economically but which, under present contracts, will close at dates between next month and the end of the winter. The communities concerned will therefore be able to rely on the continuation of present employment until the end of the next school year.
This decision is an expression of the government's declared general policy for facilitating industrial adjustments. The government is meantime vigorously exploring the opportunities for alternative employment that may be developed in these communities during the next twelve months. To attempt to bring this search to a satisfactory conclusion will be a priority activity for the department of industry, and its area development agency, whose establishment the government has proposed to parliament.

speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker. On Tuesday, the hon. member for Calgary North asked a question which I took as notice concerning the types of aircraft which have been supplied or are to be supplied to the R.C.A.F. contingent in Yemen.
On June 22 an air transport unit was formed in support of the United Nations Yemen observer mission. Aircraft from this formation are being provided by both the R.C.A.F. and the United Nations. Two R.C.A.F. Cariboo aircraft have been transferred from the United Nations emergency force at El Arish to this transport unit. In addition, the United Nations have supplied three Otter aircraft from the Congo which have been airlifted to Aden where they are being assembled by R.C.A.F. technicians and will be flown by R.C.A.F. crews to Yemen. One R.C.A.F. Otter has been temporarily transferred from UNEF to Yemen but will be returned as soon as the UN Otters are in service in Yemen.
It has also been proposed that the R.C.A.F. maintain and operate three United Nations helicopters which are presently located in the Congo. The R.C.A.F. now have a small team of technicians in the Congo examining these helicopters to determine their airworthiness. A final decision on R.C.A.F. acceptance of this helicopter commitment is being withheld pending the receipt of this technical evaluation.
To replace aircraft withdrawn from UNEF, a Dakota in Canada is being prepared for transfer to El Arish. This aircraft should be available for ferrying by approximately July 15. In addition, a Cariboo aircraft is being transferred from Trenton to El Arish effective July 8.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Tuesday of this week the hon. member for Northwest Territories asked me what was the intention of the government with respect to the furtherance of the bills providing for creation of the new territories of Mackenzie and Nunassiaq. It is our hope that we can proceed at the earliest possible moment with the resolutions, have the bills printed, and thus enable members of the House of Commons and members of the territorial council to study them. The council is meeting at Inuvik on July 8 and I think it is imperative that they be provided with copies of the bills before that time. Whether the bills should then be referred to a special committee of the house, as he suggests, is a matter for discussion and determination by the House of Commons.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. M. Drury (Minister of Defence Production):
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of Bill No. C-74 is to establish a department which will be concerned with fostering effective economic growth and development in manufacturing industry, as outlined in sections 6 and 7 of the bill. At present, Canada's manufacturing industries provide direct employment for more than one and a half million Canadians. They also create work for the many persons who are supplying materials and facilities to manufacturers. The government intends to place more emphasis on this important sector of the economy.
Traditionally, the prosperity of Canada has depended to a considerable degree on our abundant natural resources. The development of production and trade in the products of our farms, fisheries, forests and mines has been responsible for much of Canada's economic growth. In recognition of the importance of these activities, specialized departments of government have been established to work with these primary industries in order to encourage their growth on an efficient and effective basis.
The new department of industry will concentrate on the needs of manufacturing industries and will assist them in taking advantage of opportunities for sound economic development. At this time, there is probably a greater need than ever before for such a department. Canada's labour force is growing rapidly and will expand at an even faster rate in the years ahead. Many of the additional entrants to the labour force will have to find employment in manufacturing industries. Concurrent with the growth of the labour force, the accelerated trend to automation and other technological changes emphasizes the need to create new employment opportunities for substantial numbers of workers.
In recent years, we have heard a great deal about the emigration of many of Canada's skilled workers-scientists, engineers, designers and other professional and technically-skilled people. The cost of training such workers amounts to many millions of dollars each year. Many leave Canada simply because the opportunities in technically advanced industries are often greater in other
1642	HOUSE OF
Establishment of Industry Department countries. Accelerated development of manufacturing industries in Canada can help to keep these people usefully employed in Canada.
Over the past decade, the pace of technological progress in secondary industry in the more industrially advanced countries has been increasing rapidly. Progress over the next decade is certain to be even more rapid. As a result, Canada must place greatly increasing emphasis on fostering technological and economic development and growth.
The world trend to expanded trade in manufactured goods also stresses the need for effective growth in secondary industry. More and more, successful trading nations will be dependant upon vigorous and efficient manufacturing facilities as a basis for expanding their trade. Furthermore, the initiatives at present being planned to achieve an additional freeing of world trade will result in benefits for those countries which can produce competitively. On the other hand, countries which do not encourage effective development of their manufacturing industries will face increasing difficulties in meeting competition in home and export markets.
The department of industry will have a major role in implementing the government's policies to encourage effective growth and development of manufacturing. It will initiate and carry out a wide range of activities to assist manufacturing industries in improving their ability to be effective and competitive producers. In carrying out these tasks the new department will maintain a close working relationship with every sector of manufacturing. To accomplish this, the new department will have groups to work with each manufacturing industry.
The department of industry will, of course, work closely with other federal departments in implementing activities to assist manufacturing industries. It will be especially closely related from the outset to the Department of Defence Production which has been concerned with the industrial development of the defence production sector of Canadian manufacturing. It is essential, therefore, that there be very close co-operation between the two departments. The need for such a close working relationship is strengthened by the fact that the role of the Department of Defence Production is being currently reviewed in the light of the Glassco commission recommendations about consolidated government purchasing.
As the bill provides, there will be one minister who will be responsible for both departments. He will be in a position to bring about co-operation, avoid duplication of activities and achieve a meshing of the resources of the two departments. There is a


very close relationship between procurement and industrial development. For example, the Canada-United States development sharing program stresses product development and has led to the development of new exports and employment opportunities in Canada.
The government also recognizes that trade and industrial development are closely related. For this reason the department of industry will work closely with the Department of Trade and Commerce, as do other departments with specialized interests. For example, the departments of mines and technical surveys, agriculture, fisheries and forestry have special responsibilities for the growth of specific sectors of the economy. However, each of these departments also cooperates closely with the trade department in developing export markets.
It is also recognized that the provincial governments have definite responsibilities for industrial development. For this reason it is intended that the new department should work very closely with the provinces. In order to provide for effective liaison between the department and provincial governments and industry in the various regions of Canada, it is proposed to establish a number of branch offices in main regional centres.
Under section 7 (a) of the bill one of the principal responsibilities of the department will be to acquire a detailed knowledge of every aspect of manufacturing industries. Because of the increasingly close interrelationships between industry and government effective liaison is of vital importance. The department will, therefore, acquire detailed knowledge of the problems of industry and will be in a position to work closely with industry to assist in eliminating obstacles to growth and efficiency.
An important part of the liaison between the department and industry will be to provide manufacturers with a better understanding of the services which are available from government departments. These services, most of which are not available in industry itself, can often greatly assist manufacturers in overcoming problems or in finding new production opportunities. The department will seek to ensure that these services are used to the fullest extent.
Under the provisions of section 7 (b) the new department will promote the establishment, growth, efficiency and improvement of manufacturing industries in a number of ways. First, the department will assist industries to identify products which have been imported into Canada in volume and which could be manufactured in Canada on an efficient and competitive basis. In other instances it will provide information and will

Establishment of Industry Department authority to authorize and direct departments, branches and agencies of the government to undertake special measures as may be appropriate to facilitate economic development in designated areas. As a result, it will be possible to plan and implement coordinated programs involving the facilities of a number of departments. The agency also will work closely with provincial governments and regional bodies in developing and carrying out its program.
If the department of industry is to be effective, it must be in a position to acquire the services of personnel who are highly knowledgeable of the various sectors of manufacturing industry. Furthermore, it is urgent that the department have competent personnel, with specialized industry knowledge, as quickly as possible. In many instances, personnel with this type of background are not at present available in government. As a result, it will be necessary to obtain the services of a number of personnel from outside the public service during the initial stages of the department's development. Section 5 of the bill will authorize the department to employ such highly qualified persons on a temporary basis until permanent career staff can be recruited and trained in the regular manner. This special authority will terminate on December 31, 1964.
It is highly desirable that the new department should be in a position to obtain the advice of persons in industry, trade associations, organized labour and universities who have extensive background and experience in matters relating to manufacturing industries. This is particularly important in order to ensure that there is close co-operation between industry and the department. Section 15 authorizes the governor in council to appoint advisers and committees for this purpose. It is envisaged that advisory committees will be established which can be consulted respecting major activities of the department.
Through the type of activities which I have mentioned, the department of industry will have an important role in Canada's future economic development. By working closely with manufacturing industry, it will be intimately aware of industry problems and be in a position to assist effectively in their solutions. It will be concerned with technical and scientific development and the competitive advantages which Canadian manufacturers can obtain through the application of new technology. Equally important, it will be able to help manufacturers become aware and take advantage of new production and marketing opportunities. In this way, the department will be making a valuable contribution to the development of a strong and vibrant Canadian manufacturing industry.

I assume, Mr. Speaker, that if the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) had been able to be present he would have presented the government's statement on second reading of this bill. While I appreciate the minister's efforts very much, I regret that the Prime Minister has not been able to be present.
The minister gave a very detailed description of the bill, and it is this description that frightens me. In my opinion the bill illustrates the position I took during the budget debate to the effect that this government is looking towards a completely planned economy. I shall have more to say about this on some of the detailed clauses.
I was not present, unavoidably, during the debate at the resolution stage. I have, however, read all the speeches that were delivered at that time. The debate on the resolution was started, I believe, on June 7, was interrupted and then completed on June 14. There were a lot of good speeches in that particular debate but, in my opinion, one stands out. I refer to the speech delivered by the hon. member for Regina (Mr. More). This speech stands out because the hon. member cited actual experience during the latter years of the war which illustrated the useless waste of time that another bureaucracy can bring about. This is what I am afraid of in relation to this bill. The hon. member described his experience with a clothing establishment and described the waste of material and extra cost which resulted from certain directives.
The bill is now before us, Mr. Speaker, and I am sure that the fears of many hon. members, expressed at the resolution stage, have now been confirmed. Perhaps these comments should have been made during the committee stage, but I should like to point out that the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, in their report of the 92nd annual general meeting, do recommend a department of industry; but the general manager of that organization, Mr. J. C. Whitelaw, Q.C., added these remarks:
This role amply justifies the government proposal to establish a full cabinet voice for the manufacturing industry through the designation of a minister and department of industry.
But he says:
At the same time, the association has made it clear that it does not advocate the creation of yet another ministry and department, believing that the appropriate ends could be accomplished by reorganization and re-emphasis of existing facilities.
This recommendation has not been followed, Mr. Speaker, and I firmly believe it should. I believe we are setting up another bureaucratic organization which may well affect the living habits of industry in Canada to a degree where they may regret it.

We now have the bill before us and I have examined the clauses carefully. I do not intend to comment at length on the clauses at this stage because other speakers will also be addressing you on the contents of this bill. However, I do suggest we will be giving very careful consideration to the clauses of the bill as it is examined in committee. There are many clauses which will be examined quite closely. Clause 5 makes provision for the calling in of outsiders. I am wondering if we are going to have more of the three wise men from Toronto. In my humble estimation this is a very dangerous possibility. It may lead to lack of confidence in the civil service, lack of confidence in those now in the Department of Trade and Commerce who are going to be transferred to the new department of industry, and also lack of confidence in those serving the Department of Defence Production which is to be absorbed in the new department.
Are these people going to be the theoretical types? In his statement the minister said he would bring in some university people. University people are good people, but I hope he certainly gives prior consideration to those who have actually had to make a living developing industry. There is no doubt that the Minister of Finance has advocated the bringing in of what I call these wise men, but I think he has found out to his sorrow that such a step has not worked advantageously. I would hope the designate minister of industry will not allow that to happen in the new department.
In fact, Mr. Speaker, I almost suspect some of that particular theoretical type of help in the drafting of the bill. I can just see the new department commencing operations. First of all it will probably start a survey of all types of industry in Canada. Doubtlessly this will be just to get their names on file. Then the department will start a breakdown to distinguish by group, by size, and possibly by class of business. I can see the building up of a clerical system so, that despite what the Prime Minister said on resolution stage, that this was to be a department to give advice, it will become one of the greatest bureaucratic involvements in which the government has become mixed up.
After a breakdown, possibly by size or possibly by class of industry, I can see what will happen next. All sorts of circularization and questionnaires will be sent out, causing industry more headaches and much higher costs. I can just see the ideas for more and more involvement of industry in this department, sprouting like wildfire in the minds of these people who are to be brought in.

Despite what the Prime Minister said on resolution stage, that there would be no conflict of interest with the provinces, I am afraid such conflict will be demonstrated very early in the existence of the new department. With respect to the area development agency, covered in part II of the bill, 1 would point out that today the province of Ontario has this very thing in being. Will there be duplication in this respect? I can see some legitimacy, some need for something of this sort in certain areas, but I would like to know just how the area planning agency will work in with the arrangement now in force in Ontario.
Apparently very extensive powers are to be given to the new department, and a few moments ago the minister stated that other departments can be directed to do almost anything the new department suggests or thinks should be done. I am afraid of that clause. I am frightened of clause 11, as it appears to me that some official may well start telling industry what it must produce, the quantity it must produce, where it must operate, and so on. We shall have to be very careful in analysing the clauses of the bill, and we will have to get very careful and full explanations in respect to them.
Another thing which worries me somewhat is that the commissioner for area development is to report directly to the minister instead of to a deputy minister, and we will want to know just how the deputy minister of industry and the commissioner for area development will co-ordinate their efforts. Could there not be a conflict of interest between them?
I am also worried about clause 14(a). Will it be possible to get privileged information under this clause which might not otherwise be available? May the department request privileged information from other departments? We want to know exactly how far this clause commits the government, the people of Canada and industry. We must be given more explanations than the minister has thus far given in his opening remarks, and questions will be asked in due course when we come to the examination of the individual clause.
I do not like the bill, Mr. Speaker. I do not think it should be before us. Instead I think we should be setting up an industry branch under, if you like, a renamed department of trade and industry. To me this would be sufficient to give all the required information and advice. In fact it has been and is being done to quite an extent. Some years ago when the previous government set up a small business branch it was found to be of great value to small businesses throughout Canada. Also the efforts which, in the latter years of

Establishment of Industry Department the previous government, were put into developing world trade could be developed and built up within the present department. All of these things have led me to believe that there should be a branch established dealing with industry, and not a new department.
In turn this would coincide with the wishes of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association.
I think they see the pitfalls. They have stated so; and when I say that, I mean they did not advise a separate department but just a branch of the Department of Trade and Commerce. To me this would be reasonable.
I do not think I have any other matter to mention at the moment, except to say that the whole gist of the bill frightens me in that in the long run it is tending to build up another bureaucracy and another headache for industry. I just pray this does not happen.

Mr. Speaker, on behalf of our group, I would like to say what we think of the bill which has just been submitted to us by the minister who would eventually head the new department which is to be set up.
We, of the Social Credit, consider that the Canadian government is somewhat like a huge trust company with branches throughout the country, of which every Canadian is in fact a shareholder, either by birth or by naturalization. Consequently, I think that we have a certain right in this respect, and that the government's intervention in that field might help create new industries or, at least, give some guidance to firms in need of help, or rather technical or scientific assistance, which it would be possible to give them.
There are obviously some tragic things in our time. If we examine the relevant statistics, we find that within five years, more than a million new jobs will have to be created in Canada. Moreover, according to the speech from the throne, if I remember rightly, an average of 200,000 new jobs a year will have to be created.
On the other hand, I know that within three years automation will put about 15 per cent of the workers out of their jobs, and it has even been forecast that within five years, more than 25 per cent of our industrial workers will be dismissed because of automation.
We therefore have an extremely serious problem to face, because those fellow citizens, those heads of families, will have to find jobs which will enable them to support their families.
[Mr. Monteith.J
Yet, we know that there are many products we are unable to absorb at this time. Indeed, anybody can check the fact that many products remain unsold.
In several areas of industry, not to say in almost all of them, there are large stocks of products which remain unsold because Canadians do not have the money to purchase them. And all hon. members have been able to notice that in many instances. Canadians certainly do not have enough money to purchase the current production.
I agree that we must still think about creating new industries to manufacture products we do not produce at present. There are certainly many new productions we could undertake. For instance, I recall very well that a few years ago, in the Saguenay area, an important visiting economist stated that our area could accommodate over 100 industries using aluminum as a raw material. We have in our area the largest aluminum production plants in the world, and nothing is manufactured on the spot. One only has to look in the warehouses and the stores to see that there are thousands of aluminum products.
Furthermore, an industry in my riding closed down in the years 1930-1935. Yet, it would be very easy to go there and pick up molten materials by truck to bring them on the site, which would considerably reduce the cost of the products to be manufactured. Instead of using ingot aluminum, they could get it in molten form and very easily manufacture it.
This is why I am taking the liberty of suggesting to the minister that he could take this opportunity to help in our area by creating the advocated regional agencies, because we should process our raw materials, which are abundant. I believe that the regional agencies suggested in Bill C-74 may eventually encourage the establishment of new industries in our area.
Now, I hope that this department will be more efficient than some others that I have seen in operation or that, after having been set in motion, seem idle and inoperative.
I know that in the province of Quebec fine plans were made, nice programs were conceived concerning industry and commerce. But it happens that no really tangible results have been achieved at the present time.

So, I hope that this department will not be an idle department, but a department that will achieve material results, because if it is made up only of civil servants without any industrial or selling experience, without any technical experience, it will be difficult for them to achieve anything. I believe indeed that in all achievements, in all projects, you need men with practical experience.
Now I find that department will be distinct from the Department of Defence Production, which is already under the authority of the present minister. If the idea originally was to have the two departments merge, the present Department of Defence Production with that of industry, it could truly be said that we should arrive at something which would allow a really serious program to be set up, because I honestly believe those two departments ought to become one.
If I may be permitted to offer a few suggestions, Mr. Speaker, for instance I think we could include in that department of industry everything that concerns production, even the Canadian crown corporations, that is all crown corporations which produce something. Those corporations should be under the control or authority, if you prefer, of the proposed department of industry.
Thus we have Atomic Energy of Canada and many other crown corporations, such as the Polymer Corporation, which manufacture all sorts of things. Finally, those industries must be under the control of the department of industry.
There could also be a merger of anything which concerns the distribution of goods, so that it may be under the control of the Department of Trade and Commerce, because at the present time that department is concerned exclusively, or nearly exclusively, with exports. In my opinion, the Department of Trade and Commerce is a department of distribution while the department of industry is one of production. The department of production deals with production in all the fields of raw materials that one can think of, while the Department of Trade and Commerce is that of distribution and marketing. And distribution must take place. Besides, when we consider the operation of the Department of Trade and Commerce we note that it deals practically with foreign countries only whereas the Minister of Trade and Commerce should remember that Canadians are consumers who could, if they had the money or the capital needed, consume a national pro-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to speak on the second reading of this bill setting up a department of industry. I was amused to hear some of the things which have been said during this debate by spokesmen for the official opposition because I recall that remarks and criticisms of this type were made by speakers on behalf of the opposition in former days when a different government was proposing to set up a new department. There is a great deal of similarity in the arguments used.
I think this government will find itself in serious difficulty no matter what happens. They are now being charged by the opposition with being determined to go deeply into economic planning and development. They will be blamed for that, though 1 do not think they have ever seriously considered doing it. Nevertheless, they will be blamed, though they will derive none of the advantages which would follow a real attempt at economic planning. There is a crude expression which suits these circumstances very well, and the government might well find itself in such a position.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) said the other day that this new department would be to industry what the Department of Agriculture is to the farmer. This point of view was expressed again today by the Minister of Defence Production (Mr. Drury) who mentioned two other departments which are somewhat similar in nature, inasmuch as they deal with basic resources-the Department of Forestry and the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys. He also mentioned, I believe, the Department of Fisheries.
As one who comes from an inland area, I cannot speak about the Department of Fisheries and the benefits it may bring to fishermen. However, I do come from a mining area and I can say that very little advantage flows to our miners as a result of the activities of the department of mines. Neither, as yet, anyway, has much advan-


tage come to the forestry industry in my area because of the establishment of the Department of Forestry.
It is surprising to find how little relationship these departments sometimes have with the fields they represent. There is no doubt the department of mines has some of the finest buildings in Ottawa under its control. It has a large and competent staff in the department. In my area we have many problems in mining. I represent the largest silver mining community in the world and this community has for years been in serious difficulty because the department of mines, or Canada as a whole, or the industry itself have not been able to solve some of the problems which surround the production and sale of silver. It is true one can pick up a paper and see, for example, that the United States is in dire need of silver and that industry throughout the world is in need of this scarce metal. Yet we have not been able to solve the problems which arise in the area where the silver is produced. The fact is that great developments either in prospecting or in production have simply not taken place. Even the silver we produce here has to be shipped out of Canada before it is refined. Yet we are told we have one of the greatest laboratories in the world under the control of the department of mines in Ottawa.
I am using this as an example to show that unless we really know what we intend to do about an industry we can set up all the departments we like and talk about as many schemes as we wish but, in the end, nothing of practical value will have been achieved.
One thing that bothers me about the present bill is this: the minister has not yet told us what the relationship of the department will be with the economic council of Canada. Two or three years ago, the Conservative government took a forward step by setting up a council to do exactly the same as this new economic council of Canada will presumably be doing. In the period between then and now we have not really decided what the functions of this council are to be, or in which sphere it should operate. Yet, today, we are being asked to set up a department of industry to put into effect the advice which is given by the economic council of Canada. It also occurs to me that the department may find difficulty in producing enough funds to help new industry establish itself successfully.
I was interested to hear speakers preceding me talk about the advantage which Canada has in possessing certain raw materials in great abundance. I was reminded of another important industry in my area. I am thinking of cobalt. Countries such as Belgium

have established huge industries based on cobalt metal. Yet in Canada we have not even considered it worth while to develop what would be a strategic material if a future war were to be waged, and upon which rockets and atomic weapons would depend. To do this would take money, and I think it is the intention of the government to put some money at the disposal of the department of industry to assist those areas where development has not already taken place. Without any finance or provision for finance this department will be of no value at all.
I am sure the minister will say that we can ask for grants when we put forward a specific proposal, but I am thinking of some of the grants which have been given in my area. Some disgraceful things have happened in the gold mining industry just because we have never faced up to the problems. I would say that there is not one farmer in the country who could not tell you about some disgraceful things that have happened resulting from short term propositions where particular items of agricultural production were subsidized without giving consideration to other aspects of the industry. I believe this department, as the minister has said, will have to develop new industries. I think we owe a great deal of gratitude and certainly some credit to a gentleman who at one time held the portfolio of trade and commerce, Mr. C. D. Howe, for some of the things he did with regard to crown corporations, such as the Polymer Corporation. There is not a free enterpriser in this country who is not envious of the Polymer Corporation because of the fact that it has been so successful. It was completely beyond the free enterprise concept of development in the initial stages. Since then these people have not been willing to take corporations even when they were "given away for a song" as happened in the optical development industry and others. 1 think these are fields in which the department of industry will have to engage.
We have, Mr. Speaker, many resources in this country still untapped. The other day I talked to a prospector. I was interested in some advertisements I had seen concerning collectors of rocks and the large amount of money made by some of these people who look for a piece of rock which is valuable for use in other than the mineral sense. The man who stumbled on this development, which is near Perth, set up a new industry producing marble. This marble is now sent to Italy. Italian industries buy this Perth marble, to which they have given the great name of Rideau marble. A number of prospectors must have passed over that because they were only interested in gold, silver, copper, or some such mineral.
Establishment of Industry Department
There are many forms of industrial development of which advantage could be taken with the natural resources available to us, but they require development by the government. I agree that this could be done better by a department of industry than by the Department of Trade and Commerce. There always appears to be an advantage in specialization and having a mining department to handle mining and a forestry department to handle forestry. But there is no reason why they should not all be handled by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) and companion departments created but without any names. That would produce the same result, and there is a psychological advantage.
We are continually being asked to subsidize some form of industry in Canada or to give some handout; but this is not to get an industry started, to do the necessary development, or to train people to operate the industry. We are asked to give handouts to sell products which have been developed. I think this is not what we are asking for in the establishment of a department of industry. This is actually what has been done in the Department of Agriculture. The other day a farmer asked me why it was that 40 or 50 weed inspectors in his area were not able to go to the Department of Agriculture to find out which weed killers kill which weeds, and have the department give them a demonstration. They were not able to obtain that kind of assistance. But if they had asked for two or three cents more on eggs, then they would have at least had a sympathetic hearing and a favourable reply, either now or in the future. Therefore what we want is assistance to develop new industry, and this will take money which must be set aside each year.
The minister mentioned that many of these things were contemplated, and I believe it is the intention of the government to pursue them. I presume the Department of Defence Production has lost a great deal of its impetus since the war, having been built up into quite a large department. I would say that it is not an unreasonable request to put two departments under the one head. I for one express regret that we do not have the former deputy minister of defence production to assist in the development of this new industry.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. M. Fisher (Port Arthur) moved
subtopic: PROVISION FOR RETRAINING AND MOVING COSTS OF DISPLACED EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
the second reading of Bin No. C-15, to amend the Railway Act (responsibility for dislocation costs).
He said: Mr. Speaker, this bill is a small amendment to a very important act, the Railway Act, but if it were accepted it would make a tremendous change in the operations of the act and the operations of the board of transport commissioners. I believe that the bill deserves support not just for the general idea that it embodies but for the good consequences that would flow from it.
It would be preferable to me, in view of the wide interest in the bill by railroaders across Canada, that the bill be referred to the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines. Last year the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer), who was then minister of transport, indicated that this was in the mind of the government of the time, but because of the collapse of parliament this was not possible.
The fact that there is a lot of interest in the bill can be proven by the interest that members of the house in the last parliament and this parliament have shown in it, and

by the fact I have had letters from almost every province in Canada from railway workers and railway unions asking that it be implemented or, if not implemented, referred to the standing committee.
The railway association of Canada, which as most members know is made up of the management of the large railways, has examined the bill. It did this last year, and I want to be as accurate as I can. According to the information given us by the president of Canadian National Railways, Mr. Donald Gordon, when he was before our committee last year, the railway association was prepared to rebut the bill or to put its case against the bill. Therefore if the bill went to committee it would be possible to have before the committee representatives of the railway unions, certain railway communities and the railway association so that what is concerned in the bill could be examined in a very fair way.
I should like to put it to hon. members, if they are unaware of the fact, that there has been tremendous discussion over the years within railway circles about sections 181 and 182 of the Railway Act. There have been various interpretations and arguments put forward in that connection and the national legislative committee of the international railway brotherhoods year after year after year has come before the government and asked that changes be considered.
The factors that have created the demand for reconsideration can be placed in their roughest terms if one looks at the 25 year synoptical history of the Canadian National Railways as revealed in their last annual report. We find that in 1957 this railway had 124,000 employees. In 1958 the number had dropped to 113,000, in 1959 to 111,000, in 1960 to 104,000, in 1961 to 99,000 and in 1962 to 97,000. The Canadian Pacific Railway, the other major railway in Canada, and the smaller railways have had a similar dropping off in the number of employees.
This dropping off in employees reflects the tremendous changes in the make-up of the work forces and the drastic alterations in the work pattern. As a matter of fact, an employee on the maintenance of way force today is in a much different position from an employee just 10 or 12 years ago. This is so because there has been such a rapid reduction in the work force, there is so much more area for these people to cover, and there have been so many shifts. There is no area in Canada today where there is more insecurity than among railway workers.
Much of this insecurity has tended to fasten around an antagonism toward the heads of the railways, Mr. Crump and Mr. Gordon. I want to give an example of this inasmuch as I have been accused of leading

such antagonism. I wish to make the point that the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Benidickson) is credited with making the statement during the last election campaign on the platform in the town of Dryden in northwestern Ontario that after April 8 when a Liberal government took over the railway workers would not need to worry because Donald Gordon would be fired, and there would be a new sympathetic head of Canadian National Railways.
I have also noticed that there is speculation at the present time that the present Acting Prime Minister (Mr. Chevrier) is going to become president of Canadian National Railways. I do not know whether that would have happy consequences for him because it is quite obvious that being the president of the railway in these days, when the work forces and the communities that depend upon railways are so worked up over their insecurity and technological change, does not hold out a very promising future for the head of such an organization.
Before I become too sympathetic with the Acting Prime Minister, if he should assume the role, or Mr. Gordon or Mr. Crump, I should like to say that this problem needs to be approached with relative detachment and I think the railway brotherhoods have done that very well. I received a letter last fall from James F. Hutchinson, a barrister who looks after the preparation of legislation and legal material for the railway brotherhoods. He referred to this particular bill which was before parliament last session and he sent me a brief that he had prepared to be presented to the cabinet. In essence it has been put to the cabinet and I thought that if I put it on the record it would make the legal difficulties apparent and explain to hon. members the reasons that a calm consideration of these two sections is required. I might also say to hon. members that just the other day the brotherhoods presented a brief to the cabinet. I have not received a copy yet, but I think that as members of the house we all will, and I understand that this material is contained in their presentation. Mr. Hutchinson's argument in part runs this way:
Section 182 of the Railway Act provides as follows:
"The company shall not, at any time, make any change, alteration or deviation in the railway, or any portion thereof, until the provisions of section 181 are fully complied with, nor remove, close, or abandon any station, or divisional point, nor create a new divisional point that would involve the removal of employees, without leave of the board: and where any such change is made the company shall compensate its employees as the board deems proper for any financial loss caused to them by change of residence necessitated thereby."
Railway Act
I think that any hon. member reading that would say to himself that this is a tight, coherent section that means something. What have been the consequences that have flowed from it? I continue my reading:
Section 181 hereinabove referred to will be found at appendix "A".
Section 168 provides:
"The company may abandon the operation of any line of railway with the approval of the board, and no company shall abandon the operation of any line of railway without such approval."
On June 26, 1958, the Supreme Court of Canada heard a case styled "The Brotherhood of Railway Employees, James Guy McLean and J. L. McGregor (appellants) and the New York Central Railroad Company (respondent) and Canadian Pacific Railway Company and Canadian National Railway Company (intervenants)." That case dealt with an order of the Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada authorizing the New York Central Railroad Company to abandon its operation of the line of railway of the Ottawa and New York Railway Company, and authorizing the Ottawa and New York Railway Company to abandon its line of railway which extended from Ottawa to the international boundary near Cornwall, Ontario.
I am sure, Mr. Speaker, you know where that is.
The employees sought compensation under section 182 for being required to change their residence. They were denied compensation by the board, and the latter was upheld by the Supreme Court.
Mr. Justice Cartwright in a dissenting judgment stated as follows:
"The claim of the employees appears to me to fall within the words of the section construed in their ordinary meaning. The company has in fact removed, closed or abandoned every station and divisional point which was situate on the abandoned line. Those of its employees previously employed at any station or divisional point thereon who have been retained in its employment have been removed to other situations in its railway system and it has been necessary for them to change their residence. The section does not appear to have been drafted by a meticulous grammarian; but it is reasonably plain that what is conditionally forbidden by that part of the section commencing with the words 'nor remove' in the fourth line, and, if permitted, gives rise to the right of compensation in such a removal, closure or abandonment of a station or divisional point as would involve the removal of employees and necessitate a change of the residence-
In my opinion, neither the arrangement of the sections in the Railway Act nor the history of the legislation furnishes sufficient reason for failing to give to the words of the section what appears to me to be their plain and ordinary meaning".
That is the end of the quotation from Mr. Justice Cartwright's dissenting opinion.
Unfortunately, Mr. Justice Cartwright wrote a dissenting judgment and the rest of the court found that the application by the railroad company for leave to abandon had been properly made under section 168; consequently no compensation was payable to the employees by virtue of section 182.
Mr. Justice Rand stated in his judgment:
"Both in 1933 and in 1939 the question of compensation was present to the mind of the draftsman of the legislation and yet there is not a

Railway Act
word in either statute or in the Railway Act by which compensation resulting from abandonment, apart from a 'measure, plan or arrangement' between the two systems, is provided for. If that had been the intention in relation to either the Canadian National, the Canadian Pacific or any other railway acting independently under section 168, it would have been the simplest matter to provide so. It could have been done by the mere statement that the provisions of section 182 shall be deemed to apply, where the facts warrant it, to abandonment under section 168; but that step was carefully avoided. The case is one in which a feature of compensation has not been brought within a statutory provision and this court is powerless to supply it".
Then, Mr. Hutchinson goes on as follows:
It is my respectful submission that when legislation is such that two judges of the calibre of Mr. Justice Rand and Mr. Justice Cartwright cannot agree on its interpretation, an amendment should be made to the legislation. It is my submission on behalf of the brotherhoods which I represent that compensation should be provided for employees in case of abandonment and therefore I request that this committee recommend to parliament-
And so on. He goes on with his recommendations.
Now, if hon. members would look at the explanatory note in connection with this bill they would see that the purpose is to provide that railway employees, who lose their employment as a result of changes beneficial to a railway, shall be compensated by that railway for the cost of rehabilitating themselves with new skills that are saleable in the labour market; for the cost of removal expenses to a new job; pension compensation for early retirement, if that is the better plan; or such other compensation as the board deems best for the restitution of the discharged employee. A secondary amendment widens the changes contemplated by the section to include freight or express offices.
I might say, in connection with the secondary amendment, that was introduced because of plans the railways are implementing now under which they are pulling together their freight and express operations-rationalizing as it has been called-and this affects a tremendous number of employees across the country.
The general question that one might ask in relation to a hard and fast rule or law that would require a corporation to pay compensation is, what are the precedents? What does this involve? Is it putting too big an onus on the railways? This, Mr. Speaker, is something the railways need to have an opportunity of demonstrating. It is quite apparent from the announcement we had in the house yesterday -or perhaps it should have been made in the house-regarding uranium mines, that it is a conception accepted by the present government that when an industry is threatened with collapse there should be efforts made. We

had another example in the extension of coal subventions for a five-year period. As I have said, the announcement was an indication that there should be efforts made to support those people and to help them out. I have heard all the talk about the dirty dogs on the prairies who are supposed to have received too much from the overly generous previous government. I have regretted the interpretation that people outside the west are putting upon the assistance that has been given to the prairie farmers. I mention it to show that we now have accepted in a sort of piecemeal way the fact that someone should bear the responsibility for the dislocation, the wiping out of jobs, the wiping out of things that people have spent a lifetime building up, when events that are beyond their scope and beyond their planning take place.
For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, without being dogmatic about the particular wording or the virtue of the wording of the particular change that I have made, I feel that putting this before a committee and allowing for representations by a wide group that would care to come, we would be given an opportunity to deal with one of the current, lively problems that face railroaders right across the country. If the amendment or something like it were finally accepted it would, in a sense, almost be the adoption of corporate and governmental responsibility that is being accepted in this day and age when we have the effects of automation and technical change upon personnel and employment habits.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR RETRAINING AND MOVING COSTS OF DISPLACED EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak on this Bill No. C-15, I must say that I support it. I have had quite a bit to do with railway problems which, in the past four or five years, have been brought to my attention quite prominently by railway workers as a result of the continual shifting of railway policy and railway jobs. As was mentioned by the sponsor of the bill, employment on the railroads has been going down. Job security is one of the prime interests of workers on the railroads today, and they are vitally concerned about their position with the two major railroads in Canada.
We have from time to time in this house passed legislation which has had to come up for review and amendment, because as that legislation was applied to the economy of the country we found that it was not accomplishing the purpose for which it was intended. Sometimes we have found there were loopholes in this legislation which needed attention. It is my firm belief that when the Railway Act was first drawn up it was the intention of the legislators to provide compensation to employees for any financial loss. Section 182 states:

-and where any such change is made the company shall compensate its employees as the board deems proper for any financial loss caused to them by change of residence necessitated thereby.
To me this is clear; but as the previous speaker pointed out, Mr. Justice Rand and Mr. Justice Cartwright could not agree on what was meant by financial loss. Therefore when we have two noted judges who are in disagreement on a piece of legislation enacted by this house, it is certainly time that legislation was re-examined and brought before a committee of the house where the loopholes could be plugged, to bring about a greater amount of security for the workers and to ensure that they be compensated for financial loss due to shift or movement of railroad operations.
In my area there have been a number of continual movements affecting railway stations and divisional points. Divisional points are a very vital issue across western Canada, and indeed across all Canada, and the railroads have attempted to get around the provisions of section 182, which state that no divisional point shall be done away with without leave of the board and without compensation for the employees involved.
The railroads get around this provision by leaving one partial train crew at a divisional point. The point is operated by a skeleton crew until the entire crew is pensioned off, and then the divisional point slowly fades out of existence. This is what happened at Big Valley, Alberta, which was a divisional point on the C.P.R. system. Practically all the operational crews were moved out of Big Valley in the early 1920's. One crew was retained and was given a small amount of work, until finally the members of the crew were pensioned off and the point slipped out of existence. In such a case the board would not have to compensate the workers under section 182 as it now stands.
This has happened in many prairie towns. I am thinking of one in particular, the town of Mirror, where a good many years ago the railway bought the townsite and encouraged the railroad workers to buy land, settle there, and invest their savings in the town of Mirror. In those days it was maintained that the town would grow in importance; but what has happened since then? The railroad is slowly trying to do away with that town, so far as the divisional point is concerned.
Railroad workers who have invested their savings and their lifework in such towns are now finding that their land and home values are dissipating, and are practically worthless so far as resale value is concerned, because of a shift of divisional points or railroad operations generally. I do not suggest that
Railway Act
all shifts of railroad operations be stopped. I realize that with dieselization coming into effect we must be prepared to adjust to new situations, and the amendment suggested by Bill C-15 would allow for a proper adjustment with guaranteed compensation to the workers.
It is my belief that this house, or a committee of the house, should take a very close look at this crucial and anxious problem. Just the other day I asked the Minister of Transport a question pertaining to divisional point run-throughs. I asked the minister would he take it upon himself to consult the C.N.R. and stop any proposed run-throughs until the next wage negotiation contracts were up. He replied no, that he did not feel this would be a proper undertaking for him to give. That illustrates part of the uncertainty which railroad workers are facing. They do not know if this falls under their wage contracts, whether it should be a part of railroad management, or just exactly where it falls.
The proposed amendment embodied in Bill C-15 would go a long way toward creating a certain amount of guaranteed compensation and a certain amount of security in railroad employment. A few years ago if a worker had 10 or 12 years seniority with a railroad he had a certain amount of security, but today 10 years seniority is not enough to guarantee any security.
It has been pointed out previously that there are now something like 97,000 people employed by the railways, compared with 120,000 a few years ago. What the hon. member is seeking in his proposed amendment to section 182 is a certain amount of security in compensation, and I wholeheartedly support him in suggesting that the bill be referred to the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, where both sides of the argument could be heard. In that committee we might come up with an amendment similar to the one in this bill, and which would accomplish the same end.
I conclude by saying I certainly think this should be referred to a committee, and the committee should review it as a matter of urgency in order to bring some clarification to the act. Such clarification would be very beneficial to all railroad employees across Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-15 is most significant and we readily agree that it should be referred to the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, so that it can be fully looked into.

Railway Act
If we duly keep in mind what has happened over the last ten years, we find that railways have modernized locomotives. I remember very well that in 1959, in Quebec, it was decided to make some changes on account of automation and over 50 locomotives even had to be sent to Montreal in order to be serviced. At that time, of course, some workers from Quebec, who had been with the railways for a number of years, had to be transferred to Montreal. Others had been laid off, since there was no outside work for them.
As late as April 15 last, in Limoilou, certain changes had to be made, with the result that further Quebec employees had to move to Montreal, and eight of them had to be laid off for lack of work.
Though we may not be personally averse to automation, we must not forget that some workers have been sacked, and have thus experienced a sharp drop in their living standards.
That is why it is essential that the bill be referred to the committee on railways, so that all its clauses and possibilities might be explored, in order that the company might direct its employees to other sectors, thus avoiding a recurrence of the undesirable patterns of the past.
I have before me some resolutions passed by various union locals against the railways' decision to dismiss some of their employees in a near future.
If we take a look at the lower St. Lawrence region, we will find that over there they have adopted the "master-agency" system, resting on a master-agent. This method is being given a trial around Moncton, and if it proves successful, it will be used from east to west. This would mean that nearly 1,300 workers and employees of the C.N.R. would lose their jobs, and that their families would naturally suffer.
So, Mr. Speaker, it is most important that this bill be referred to the railways committee so that the employees who are laid off may find work in other fields and may have a minimum of security.
Automation is a very good thing but we must look after the employee, who is an asset for Canada; if we are concerned only with automation at the expense of workers, we will be faced with serious problems.
The house adopted last year a bill to assure the mobility of labour in the industry, and I think that charity begins at home. So, we must provide labour mobility within crown corporations as well as within industry.

So, Mr. Speaker, we entirely agree that this bill be referred to the railways, canals and telegraph lines committee for a more thorough study.
