speakeroldname: Mr. Hubert Badanai (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works
subtopic: PROVISION FOR RETRAINING AND MOVING COSTS OF DISPLACED EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is a bill which merits consideration, and I am indeed happy to rise in support of the principle, which will provide a measure of compensation to railway employees when the railway management decide on changes which may be beneficial to them, but which could work a real hardship on the employee if it involves removal from one location to another or a change of job. The purpose of this amendment moved by the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) is to provide that railway employees who lose their employment as a result of changes beneficial to a railway shall be compensated by that railway for the cost of rehabilitating themselves with new skills, etc. This will also affect the non-operating employees of the railway.
During the past few years there has been a concerted move to effect so-called savings by unification of railway services of one kind or another. At the lakehead, in Fort William we have seen the unification of the telegraph offices which are now being jointly operated as one. This is contrary to statements and promises made at the time-this happened about two and a half years ago- that it would not mean loss of jobs, when protests were advanced against the amalgamation. The truth of the matter was revealed later, after the deal was consummated. It did mean loss of employment and loss of opportunity for some of those who had been in the telegraph service of the two railways. Years ago Sir Edward Beatty, who was president of the Canadian Pacific Railway, initiated a movement of amalgamation of the railways. He travelled up and down the country speaking in support of this idea which, to the credit of the government of Mackenzie King, was successfully resisted; and as far as I am concerned, any such move should be resisted now.
From time to time we read comments, statements and editorials suggesting that competition for railways is no longer required. I wish to quote an editorial which appeared in The Nation's Business magazine as an example of the thinking of some people in the country at the present time:
It is most difficult to demonstrate that there exists now a need for two railway systems in Canada. The alternative to the continued payment

of subsidies is to wind up, by government action, the railway undertaking of either the C.N.R. or the C.P.R.
This plea for railway amalgamation, which comes from transportation specialist Richard Rohmer, Q.C., at least has the decided virtue of freshness and bluntness.
The editorial continues:
The rail problem is one which in Canada has had a minimum of hard, twentieth century thinking. For a long time the two rail system has been widely defended or tolerated on the assumption that in the rail industry, as in other industries, competition is a vital working force in maintaining maximum incentives to efficiency.
That view was justified in bygone days when the railways had what amounted to a monopoly in long distance transportation. But given competition from new ways of moving goods and people, the theory of competition for railways needs candid review.
I do not share these views, Mr. Speaker, because I believe that in the long run the railways would stand to lose, rather than gain, by amalgamation. On the other hand, the problem facing the grain trade in western Canada, where there is the proposed wholesale abandonment of branch lines by the railways which have been serving approximately 1,000 country elevators, is a serious one and very careful consideration will have to be given to this question before taking definite steps. It has been reported that not only will the grain companies suffer capital losses through a reduction of storage revenue and disruption of handling grain, but hundreds of men will be without jobs, including elevator and railway employees. The farmer, too, will be affected by having to haul his grain to the main line, which may be anywhere from 15 to 50 miles further away.
According to a survey of consumer expenditures in 1950 prepared by the bureau of labour statistics of the United States department of labour, the loss of 100 railway jobs would have the following effects upon a community: $52,300 paid by the workers in taxes would be lost as income to support the community and the nation; $159,600 spent for food and beverages would be lost to local grocers and restaurants; $9,300 less would be spent for tobacco. Well, this item may of course please the hon. lady the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss LaMarsh). Forty-nine thousand eight hundred dollars less would be spent for rent and other housing costs; $19,800 in business would be lost to producers of electric power and sellers of fuel and refrigeration; $19,800 less would be spent for things necessary to operate a household; $41,600 worth of business would be lost by furniture and household equipment dealers. Sixty thousand dollars less would be spent for clothes and clothing services; $87,000 less would be spent for transportation, including automobiles, servicing, gas and oil; $24,000 less would go as income to doctors,
Railway Act
nurses and others providing medical care; $11,000 less would be spent in beauty parlours and in the sale of cosmetics; $34,000 less would be spent on recreation, education and books; $6,000 less would be spent with miscellaneous business, $19,000 less would be given as gifts to churches and other institutions, and $24,000 in premiums for personal insurance would be lost to insurance salesmen.
Then, as the population of the world grows-and we are told that 40 years from now the population will be doubled-Canada's role in feeding the world will increase in importance and the need for an intensified production of grain will be evident. I can see a real need for the intensive cultivation of land, not for the abandonment of railway lines, a step which I consider can only produce unemployment and inconvenience, at best. As Canada's population grows, the troubles of the railways will disappear. That is my personal view.
In the meantime, we must develop and advance solutions to counteract prospective job losses due to automation, and the bill before us appears to offer to the railroads a reasonable proposal which would cover specific situations, being a broad protective measure for the benefit of those who through no fault of their own may be thrown out of a job or forced to move into an unfamiliar type of work which would require retraining.
The railways, certainly, have obligations to those of their employees affected by reason of the adoption of labour saving installations such as automatic yards, or office machinery, or indeed because of abandonment of branch lines or reduction of services. In all of these moves there should be, first, maximum notice of intention. Where displaced employees have no opportunity to relocate with the company, the railways should assume the responsibility of looking after them and their families until a satisfactory relocation is possible.
In other countries, such as England and the United States, there are arrangements for financial assistance for employees of railway companies who are required to relocate their homes as a result of changes in operations. In addition, there are schedules of severance pay for those who are unfortunate enough to lose their employment as a result of such changes. Without going into great detail, these countries give recognition to the human consequences resulting from technological change and other innovations.
The present Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) speaking in Selkirk, Manitoba on March 8, 1963, made a statement on railway branch line policy which I should like to quote. The
references within it to the prime minister-

Railway Act
as he was, then-are, of course, references to the hon. member for Prince Albert, now Leader of the Opposition.
I am aware that the entire structure ol the Canadian transportation system is changing. This is particularly true of western Canada. Many of the changes being made are essential, but we must be sure that when changes are made, they are not made at the undue expense of particular areas and particular population groups.
The national government has an important responsibility where transportation is concerned because transportation is a foundation stone of Canada's social and economic life.
The Liberal party has given close attention to this issue. We will, when we form a government, see that any changes made are made with foresight and only after the fullest consideration of the interests of all those affected. We will ensure that essential branch line services are maintained.
A few years ago the Prime Minister appointed a special royal commission on transportation. After much study, the commission reported. One sentence from the report reads: "We are, therefore, in no position to offer a detailed plan for the rationalization of Canada's railway plant." Since that report came out, nothing has been done. Now, within the last few days, the Prime Minister has suggested that he has the answers. He says he is going to set up a branch line rationalization fund. It is true the royal commission could not solve the branch line problem. Now, after six years of delay the Prime Minister would have us believe he is going to take action.
The Liberal party does not claim to have all the answers to this very difficult problem. However, we will tackle it intelligently and without delay. As a government, the Liberals will establish a committee of inquiry to receive representations from farmers, labour, the municipalities and the provinces. This committee will be responsible for studying all the social and economic implications involved in the suspension of railway services. It will consider these implications not only from the standpoint of the railway companies but from the standpoint of the benefit to farmers, businessmen and the community in general. It will, as a government, be careful that no hasty actions are taken while the committee is deliberating. When the committee reports, its reports will be the foundation of a railway policy based on the best interests of all concerned groups and designed to maintain essential branch line services.
It seems to me that this statement is a fair appraisal of the situation. The Prime Minister is conscious of the consequences of any policy which would mean the displacement of workers in industry, and this includes layoffs in the railways. I trust that before this private members' hour expires, the Solicitor General (Mr. MacNaught) will consider moving a motion referring this measure to the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines for further study. I believe in a railway policy which would give every man employed with the railway company an opportunity to continue to work and also the chance of a better life than has been possible in the past several years as a result of dislocation, lay-offs and other troubles which appear to be the order of the day.

speechtext:
I rise briefly to express my wholehearted support for the principle and purpose of this bill. I do so because I have been interested in this question for a number of years particularly as a result of living in a district where mining is an important occupation. I am also interested in this as one who has seen the loss suffered by miners because of mines being worked out. I can think of one community which had a thousand inhabitants some 20 years ago. Now, it has only seven. I can think of others which had three or four thousand workers or residents but which today are reduced to populations of three or four hundreds because of the change in circumstances brought about by a changing pattern in the mining industry. I noticed the inconvenience and loss suffered by these miners before I was a member of any legislature and before I became a member of the House of Commons. It may be of interest to the house that the mine, mill and smelter workers union was to my knowledge the first union in Canada to urge this principle because of their experience with mining industry development. The government and corporations should, Mr. Speaker, accept some responsibility for losses encountered through loss of employment as a result of closing down of mines. It may also interest the house to know that there are two members of the mine, mill and smelter workers union in this house. One is the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Byrne) and the other is the hon. member for Kootenay West, and we are both proud of our membership.
I am of the opinion, Mr. Speaker, that both the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) and the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Badanai), as well as other speakers, have expressed the need for this measure very well indeed. Mr. Speaker, when discussion of this bill was interrupted at five o'clock I was dealing with some of the problems that this group would like to bring to the minister's attention on the second reading of Bill No. C-74, an act respecting the establishment of a department of industry. We think that this bill can be a very good one and that the department of industry can be very acceptable to the Canadian people or the measure can be a very innocuous one depending on how the administration of the department operates.
I believe the Canadian people are aware of the fact that our economy is rapidly changing, that industry is going to play a much more important part in our economy year by
Establishment of Industry Department year and that a department to assist industry to develop and to establish the trade patterns needed to sell its products can be very ueeful. If the department operates like some of the other departments having to do with basic industries such as agriculture, forestry, mining and fisheries, then this will not really be earthshaking legislation. If, however, the minister puts all his known attributes behind making this new part of his responsibility his prime function, then I am quite sure that the department of industry can be very valuable. I am quite sure that this will be done. However, unless there is a willingness to give consideration to some of the problems that have been raised there are going to be many years of frustration before this department functions in the way that it should.
I was at the opening of an institution for the training of young people and the retraining of unemployed persons and I was very surprised to hear one of the officials make the startling statement that it is all right to come and represent the federal government and the contribution it is making, but what are we doing about getting the United States to make a contribution? I think we in Canada have made a contribution to the United States in that many of our people who have obtained their technical training and knowledge here have gone to that country because of our inability to maintain the industries we already had, or to establish new ones. One excellent example was our inability to cope with the problem of the technical staffs we had trained for the aircraft industry at the time of the development of the CF-105. At that time we had in Canada some of the best technical advisers and most competent technical people in the aircraft industry anywhere in the world. Yet almost overnight we lost a great percentage of these people because of our inability to take advantage of the knowledge they had.
I believe that this new department is very worth while. It is one that can serve the needs of the people. The charge was made by the Conservatives this afternoon that the department will not function properly because the present government is going into the field of economic planning, and that this will be detrimental. In my opinion the department will succeed if the government does go into the field of economic planning, assesses the situation from the point of view of the benefit to the Canadian people and then makes its economic planning work. We are setting up a council to provide knowledge of what is needed. Now we are setting up a department to make effective use of this knowledge. I believe that the minister should give consideration to having money provided for the department by way of a statutory item

Mr. Speaker, in rising to support and urge second reading of this bill I must first comment that I was struck by the theme, the keynote almost, of of the remarks of the hon. member for Perth (Mr. Monteith) who spoke for the opposition. His keynote might be exemplified by the word "frightened". He said he was frightened by a certain clause. He said we had to be very careful about some other part of the bill. This attitude exemplifies the all too well known Conservative approach to the whole problem of industrial development in Canada, and especially the problem of the development of certain areas that have been lagging behind in economic growth and progress.
With this attitude of fear, of overcarefulness if I may call it that, it is no wonder that year after year during the six years of the Tory regime we had a hard core of hundreds of thousands of unemployed. It is no wonder that unemployment averaged over 6 per cent a year. Either they ignored this problem completely and suggested that it did not exist or, if they recognized it, instead of using the approach which we see in the bill before us today, especially the provisions for an area development agency, they used a fragmentary, bits and pieces approach -an order in council here, a special tariff exemption there or the removal of some other exemption in some other place. Instead of settling down and tackling the whole problem as a matter of national policy they were content, as I say, either to ignore its existence on just to nibble around the edges.
I say that it is about time we recognized, as is done in the present bill, that there are areas in all parts of our country that have lagged behind for years in respect of economic development. Because of changing technology and shifts in the national economy and through industries leaving certain areas, we find that there are parts of our country where there is a hard core of thousands of people unemployed year after year. Unfortunately the former government, in spite of ample opportunity and in spite of the fact that this problem was brought very forcibly to their attention by people now on the government side and by representatives from these areas, did little or nothing about it.
The problem of the depressed areas has many serious effects on the municipalities concerned. The municipalities are faced with heavy burdens for relief and social assistance.


They are faced with the burden of carrying the indebtedness brought about by having to pay for roads, sidewalks and schools that they built for the benefit of the workers in factories which then decided to move to other areas of our country.
Probably most important of all was and is the human factor, the effect upon people whose jobs, after years of working, have suddenly disappeared, leaving them in communities where there is little or no hope of finding other employment, leaving them with the problem of continuing to pay for homes into which they put their entire savings, leaving them without training to make use of even any new jobs where such jobs exist. Surely, it must be obvious by now, as I know it is when we see this bill presented to this house, that if we can pay the money we do for relief, for unemployment insurance, it is equally sensible to carry out incentive measures through the medium of a body such as the area development agency of this new department of industry, to stimulate industry so as to provide this needed employment in those areas that have been lagging behind the rest of our country.
After all, Mr. Speaker, eight countries of western Europe, and the United States as well, have by now recognized the usefulness of special programs for area development. It is important to recognize, as has been recognized by the presentation of this bill, the need for a broad national policy. The hon. member for Perth (Mr. Monteith) referred to efforts being made in Ontario. Surely, he must recognize that there is a lot more to Canada than Ontario, even though my own community is in one particular corner of it. All provinces are not equally able to act in this field or, for that matter, equally willing to act. The federal government's taxing powers, its fiscal and monetary powers, will be powerful weapons to fight this chronic unemployment that we have had too long, wherever it may be found in our Canadian nation.
In urging second reading of this bill, Mr. Speaker, I suggest that we have to consider this bill as part of a great program to rebuild confederation. There has been a lot of talk inside and outside of this house about the need, as we approach the centenary of the founding of this nation, to do something about the repairing of the tears that have come into its fabric. I think that many others have pointed out that some of these tears, these strains, have come through economic causes. If we are to rebuild confederation, as we must, it is necessary not only to make sure that we have fair treatment for the peoples of both basic cultures of this country,

but also to make sure that we have fair treatment in the economic sense of people from every corner of this nation, whether they be from my own community of Windsor, Elliot Lake, Gaspe or any other part of our country. In this way, we will carry out the essential task before us of rebuilding confederation and thereby being able to celebrate the centenary of the nation in 1967 in the most appropriate way. Mr. Speaker, I urge the prompt second reading and implementation of this bill.

Mr. Speaker, unlike the hon. member who has just preceded me, I would like to talk about Bill C-74 which deals with the department of industry. This bill proposes establishing a department that is going to be dealing with industry in our country.
I think first of all we must always ask ourselves, in looking at a proposal such as this where we are thinking of the government taking some action with respect to a private segment of the economy, if there is a need for the government to become involved in this type of activity. I think we on this side of the house feel-I know I certainly do- that those things that can be done by industry should be done by industry, without government interference. The government should only become involved if there is a need, if there are problems that industry itself cannot solve.
In the case of our industry now, there is ample evidence that some action by the government is required. Let us look at a few factors in connection with our industry.
First of all, we know that many people in this country depend on industry for their jobs. We also know that we have large-scale unemployment, and that therefore industry has not been able to provide the necessary jobs. This is true despite the fact that last year we had a large scale increase in industrial activity.
We also know that we will have many new people coming into the work force over the next few years, and we are going to have problems as automation releases people from their jobs. So that the situation is not going to get better; it will get worse.
We know as well that our industry must export, and increase its exports, if it is going to expand sufficiently to provide the necessary growth that will ensure the necessary jobs. If we are to export and compete in world markets we know we can only do so on two bases: We either have a unique product to sell, or we have low prices.
What about our industry at present? A large segment of it does not do its own designing. A large segment depends, through licensing arrangements, on designs done outside our country. In addition much of our industry is producing at the relatively low volume levels of our own domestic market, and hence it has the high costs that go with such a volume. A large segment of our industry has therefore neither the unique design

nor the low costs that will enable it to compete successfully in world markets.
We also know that many millions of dollars worth of parts, bits and pieces, are imported by industry for assembly into finished products in this country. A percentage of these could, and should be made in Canada if we are to cut down on our unemployment and provide the requisite number of jobs.
These are problems that exist now, and they are problems that will become even more severe as trends toward freer trade develop. Our industry is having problems providing enough jobs under current conditions. As tariffs come down, and as trade becomes freer, these problems will increase. Our industry has not yet solved the problems that will enable it to compete under these new conditions.

I prefer to finish my speech first. Industry has not solved these problems by itself, and this I believe is sufficient justification for government help in this field. In fact I feel that if the government does not help in this field it will be negligent in its responsibility to the people of the country.
I believe industry recognizes this, that it welcomes government help, and that it welcomes the establishment of a department of industry. Despite the remarks of the hon. member for Perth (Mr. Monteith), I am sure the Canadian Manufacturers' Association would like to see this department established.
It is not going to be the job of this department-indeed nothing in the bill implies it- to interfere with industry and strangle it with red tape. It is not the purpose of the proposed department, as the hon. member for Timis-kaming (Mr. Peters) suggested, to subsidize uneconomic segments of our industry. Neither do I believe it is, nor should it be, the purpose of this department to act as a government consultant or lending bureau for individual companies that have fallen behind the times and have got themselves into trouble.
To me the purpose of the new department is to do two main things, as set out in the bill. First of all, it is the job of the department to learn the facts, to find out what the situation is, and to identify and set up the problems. Having done that, its job is to work out, with industry, solutions to these problems. This task can only be done and the solutions can only be posed once the problems have been identified in specific terms.
The first stage, therefore, must be a detailed industry by industry examination to determine these problems. The hon. member for Perth suggested there would be a blizzard of paper and forms. He suggested that statistics

Establishment of Industry Department would be compiled and counter compiled, and filed and counterfiled. I believe many of these statistics presently exist, and I think the minister designate, and the persons who will work with him in the new department, will have reasonable powers of logic and normal portions of common sense. I would expect that the industries would be selected on some rational basis. I would imagine there would be some priority in selecting these industries, and that priority presumably would be based on those industries that might yield the greatest returns first.
I would assume, for instance, that such things as total employment in an industry would be one of the criteria, for those industries that have now large scale employment are the ones that offer the most immediate potential gains in future employment. I think another criteria in selecting industries would probably be the volume of imports, because here is the plum that we want to pick; these are the items that, if we can make them here, offer relatively immediate gains in employment. Also, obviously the export potential of an industry would help to determine the order in which it is selected. This industry by industry study, as the minister has stated, has already started with the automobile industry.
The hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) has been asking where the money is; why do we not pour in millions of dollars. I do not believe that this department should become a means through which we wind up with socialized industry in this country. I think that wherever possible the solutions to the problems that are posed should be achieved through normal financing channels. This will not always be possible, and if funds are needed for special projects I believe these funds should be appropriated as required. To my mind it is better to ask for the funds and appropriate them as you need them, rather than set up a large sum of money which you then scurry around trying to find ways and means of spending. While on the subject of financing, I would hope that this department would have a close liaison with the industrial development bank so that this agency which is already in existence might be of more help, particularly to some of the smaller industries in the country.
The hon. member for Perth (Mr. Monteith) opposed the idea of the department at the beginning of his speech, but toward the end I believe he recognized, as I am sure other hon. members do, the need for this work, because he suggested, as others have, that it should be carried out through the Department of Trade and Commerce and that this department should be expanded to become
1662	HOUSE OF
Establishment of Industry Department a department of trade and industry. Let us look at the Department of Trade and Commerce. It is now acting to some degree as a sales agency in foreign markets for our farm produce, for the Department of Agriculture, for our forestry products, and our mineral products. It is working in the field of export sales of our oil and gas; it is arranging tariff negotiations of great importance to the large scale development of this country. I think this department as it is now constituted has quite enough to do. I believe that even though the minister is extremely capable, he has enough to do. I mentioned at the resolution stage that there was general agreement in Canada that emphasis should be placed on the development of industry. No one finds any fault with that at all. I quoted from the dominion bureau of statistics Canada Year Book for 1962 a paragraph indicating the development of Canada as an industrial nation. Everyone is seized with the importance of industry. I had intended at that time-and I take the opportunity of doing so now-to point out that, although we hope to gain greater employment through the development of industry, we must not be carried away by any misconceptions with regard to employment based on industry. It is absolutely essential to have industries and to have more of them, but it does not necessarily follow that employment on a large scale results from the multiplication of secondary manufacturing. I wish that were the case; but improved methods of manufacturing and automation seem to have slowed the rate of employment in manufacturing. When you look at page 616 of the Canada Year Book for 1962 you find it gives a summary of manufactures from 1917 to 1960. You find that-I will take two years for comparison -in 1953 there were 38,107 manufacturing establishments in Canada. By 1959, the other year for comparison, the number of manufacturing establishments had declined to 36,193. If we look at the employment factor in 1953, we discover there were 1,327,451 people employed in those manufacturing establishments. In 1959, the number was 1,303,956. It is interesting to note that the productivity factor has been good. The gross value of products increased from almost $18 billions in 1953 to $23 billions in 1959. Thus, improved methods of manufacturing have brought about increased productivity but the employment factor has not shown the great increase which perhaps we all hoped it would.
Similar material is given in the Canada Year Book with regard to the provinces and

with regard to the leading manufacturing industries. It shows a steady growth in the industrialization of Canada but this growth does not reflect the increase in employment for which we might have hoped. Percentage distribution of employed, by industrial groups, shown on page 711, indicates the point I have been stressing. In 1961, of a total number employed of some six million people, 11 per cent were in agriculture, 3 per cent were in other primary industries, 25 per cent in manufacturing, 6.7 per cent in construction, 8.4 per cent in transportation and other utilities, 16.3 per cent in trade, 4 per cent in finance, insurance and real estate, and 25.5 per cent in various services. If we compare with these figures the situation in 1961 we will see that there has been a sharp decline in the total employed in agriculture. In other primary industries, the decline is about 1 per cent. In manufacturing, the percentage has stayed close to 25 per cent as it has done for many years. In the construction industry it has stayed between 6.5 and 7 per cent. Transportation has run around 8 or 8.5 per cent; employment in trade has increased by about 1.5 per cent. But the big increase has occurred in the service industries, employment in which has risen in a period of ten years from 18 per cent of the total employed to 25.5 per cent.
That is the way employment is running in our country at the present time. My criticism of the bill, and of the whole idea, is that the Department of Trade and Commerce, as it is at the present time, is equipped to do all that the proposed department of industry is aiming to do. speechtext:
I was drawing attention to the reorganization which took place in the Department of Trade and Commerce for the express purpose of recognizing the importance of industry and of secondary manufacturing in this country. The people engaged in secondary manufacturing came to Ottawa and prior to the appointment of an assistant deputy minister in charge of domestic commerce, as it is called here, they made their visits to the Department of Finance. In those days officials of the Department of Finance familiar with matters pertaining to industry were selected to receive them. In those days, too, officials of the Department of National Revenue were available for consultation and advice but the situation appears to have changed recently. I found that representatives of secondary manufacturing paid their visits to the Department of Trade and Commerce, not solely for the purpose of getting information and assistance or of putting forward ideas with regard to Canada's export trade but also to look for help and guidance in the domestic field and in the industrial development of Canada. It seemed we should have someone to meet the representatives of the manufacturing industries when they came to

Establishment of Industry Department Ottawa, hence the appointment of an assistant deputy minister in the Department of Trade and Commerce. If the Department of Trade and Commerce were renamed the department of industry and commerce-because the words "trade" and "commerce" are practically synonymous, the problem which faces us now will be met. Moreover, the emphasis will be placed on industry as, indeed, I agree it should be. The department as now set up is fully qualified to give industry the assistance it needs. That has been proved over the years. It is one of the oldest departments of government, one of the best organized, contains a large number of people who have had vast experience in dealing with industrial problems, and it has a first class group of trade commissioners posted around the world who keep constantly in touch with people engaged in industry here wishing to enter the export market.
To my mind setting up a department of industry at this stage would strike at the Department of Trade and Commerce and weaken it. I regret that the present Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp) has not taken a firm stand on this and held his department together and intact. I do not understand why he permits a slicing away of a very important segment of his department and having it placed under this new department of industry, because there is an integration within that department. Secondary industry is interested in the export field just as are the primary industries, and with our small population of about 19 million we have not the base to enlarge our industrial production as we would wish. Therefore, increasingly the manufacturing industries are looking to the export market in order to get a wider field for their products. Within the Department of Trade and Commerce, with an assistant deputy minister whose sole aim in life is the production of the interests of industry and whose associates are engaged in promoting export trade abroad, are a group of officials able to undertake this task. To set up a separate department of industry strikes, as I say, at one of the very strong departments of government, and in my opinion weakens it, and weakens it unnecessarily.
I know, Mr. Speaker, from the experience which I had with that department, of the close association there is between those who are engaged in secondary manufacturing and those who are interested in export trade. The Department of Trade and Commerce over the last several years has been busily engaged in doing some of the things which the government now proposes shall be done by the department of industry. In one of the clauses of the bill we read that:

The minister shall
(a) cause the department to acquire a detailed knowledge of manufacturing industries in Canada;-
-as if that is something which had not been done in the past, and is opening up a new frontier.

The government is now starting to acquire through a new department a detailed knowledge of manufacturing industries in Canada. That knowledge has already been in the possession of departments of government, particularly the Department of Trade and Commerce. In that department over the last several years a survey has been conducted with regard to imports coming to this country in an endeavour to classify those articles imported from abroad which could and should be manufactured within this country. That information has now been assembled and transmitted to secondary manufacturers in this country, so the very thing the new department is expected to carry out has already been done. The same clause says that the minister shall-
-promote the establishment, growth, efficiency and improvement of manufacturing industries in Canada-
Mr. Speaker, that is what the Department of Trade and Commerce through that special branch has already been working at. Then-
-to assist the adaptation of manufacturing industries to changing conditions in domestic and export markets-
The Department of Trade and Commerce under the assistant deputy minister of domestic commerce has already been doing that. Then-
-to identify and assist those manufacturing industries that require special measures to develop an unrealized potential or to cope with exceptional problems of adjustments-
That must have been written by an outside adviser. The Department of Trade and Commerce has already been doing that. Then lastly, the same clause says that the minister shall-
_promote the development and use of modern
industrial technology in Canada and improve the effectiveness of the participation by the government of Canada in industrial research.
The Department of Trade and Commerce has already been interested in that particular problem. So that here we have the truncating of one of the largest and most important departments of government; the formation of a new department which will have thrust into

its midst, apparently, the Department of Defence Production, and then will have added to that a development agency, diverting it from the task which we would expect it to undertake.
So, Mr. Speaker, on those grounds I suggest that there is still time for the government, fumbling and bumbling and uncertain as it is, to make the corrections to this bill, wipe out the department of industry section of it, rename the Department of Trade and Commerce the department of industry and commerce, strengthen it if you like, and then set up this agency development program to assist those areas in need of special assistance.
I said at the resolution stage, Mr. Speaker, that my experience was that if bills were carefully prepared and carefully drafted there was little difficulty in getting them through the House of Commons, and I have the records for several years which I have studied to indicate that. The House of Commons loses time on other matters, but not on legislation, except in instances where the legislation is badly drafted; and in this instance the legislation has been badly drafted. It was a hurried-up job and we have presented to us now a bill which in many respects is thoroughly unsound.
I suggest that the government take a little time now-they may have 120 days and not just 60 for further plans-to pause and reflect and study the problem again. Do not destroy part of the effectiveness of the Department of Trade and Commerce, which I think is the most serious thing that is going to happen under these circumstances. Because if the government blindly goes ahead and sets up a new department of industry, is it then going to transfer from the Department of Trade and Commerce the people who are working there in the fields about which I have already spoken? Or is the government going to bring in outsiders? There are some temporary appointments to be made apparently-persons having special knowledge to advise the minister. These temporary people called in from outside is a matter we will discuss in committee.
In the Department of Trade and Commerce you have men who have grown up with the problem; people who have been selected after graduation from university, given a course of training and brought into the department. There are many men there who have had years and years of experience and know more about industry in Canada than, I would say, the members in this chamber and most other people in the country. They have a broad view of the whole problem and they know the implications and the changes which are desirable and which should be made. These are the men who also have knowledge of the 28902-5-106

So I suggest that even at this stage the government should reconsider the matter and revise their plan. The revision that I suggest will not destroy the idea at all. I reiterate that everybody in Canada is in favour of emphasizing industrial development and we have no objection to that at all. I do not think there will be serious objection with regard to the other problem of helping certain designated areas where the employment situation may be improved by industrial assistance. Within the presently organized government departments the agencies are there for industrial development. In the Department of Trade and Commerce there are experienced men. A change of name only might be necessary, or alternatively raise the administration of the industry side to the status of a deputy minister and have a deputy minister in charge of industry and a deputy minister in charge of the other facets of the department now known as trade and commerce. That would elevate and give emphasis to industrial development rather than the government creating another portfolio and plucking another minister out of the hat to develop a new department, thus multiplying the bureaucratic controls to which objection has already been taken in the house.
Those are some of my objections, Mr. Speaker, to the way in which this proposal has been put before the House of Commons. I do not object to the proposal but I do object to the way in which it has been presented.

To illustrate those facts, I cannot do any better than read to you an extract of an article by Hr. Lorenzo Pare, former president of the press gallery here, in L'Action of March 29; I quote:
The village closing round the steeple, against a background of mountains along the seashore. A community united through work and virtue. Under the powers mentioned by the bill before us, there is, on the one hand, a provision for research on the problems particular to underdeveloped areas to help them and to co-ordinate efforts within each department to bring about an efficient action which will redress our economy and put an end to the exodus of healthy young people from small centres to large cities.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill that we have before us tonight is aimed at filling a great need in Canada.
I take exception to the way the bill is drafted because it appears to provide more government by pigeon hole. It appears to be trying to set up an economic dictatorship. We have to back away from the subject and take a look at the over-all proposition. We must ask ourselves, are we prepared for national socialism, or are we not. If we are not, then I think we should redraft this bill and take a new look at ideas of economic planning. The sweeping powers which the minister would be given if the bill became law would make him the virtual dictator of all businesses in Canada.
If the purpose of the bill were devoted to government planning with a view to advising businesses how best to run their affairs, I would be all in favour of it; but if it is to set up a master crown corporation wherein all businesses large and small, will be dictated to by government of any kind at any level, then I would throw the bill out. I am not prepared for anything like national socialism of any kind.
I believe there is a great need for more investigation and exploration into the natural resources of our country; but as the house well knows, these are largely in the control of the provincial governments and so we would need, as outlined in clause 14(b), the approval of the governor in council to enter into agreements with the various provincial governments. This is not an easy task. I have had some experience in this regard with the Social Credit government of Alberta, and it is difficult even to make contact with them, to have them meet in any friendly way to discuss the over-all problems of developing the natural resources in that fair province.
To suggest that the minister have jurisdiction only over those things which come under federal jurisdiction would restrict us to the development of industry in the Northwest Territories, and although the Northwest Territories are a very important part of Canada, it seems to me it is the over-all development of our natural resources which is required. Probably the best way of accomplishing that is by setting up a board in complete co-operation with the provinces, for our industrial development, and making use of our natural resources.
Of course the bottleneck will be the credit necessary to develop these resources. It has


been suggested by one minister that we do not need to set up a large fund for the development of these resources. Therefore we are going to have large plans without anything behind them. Again I say we should drop this idea of government by pigeon hole. What we need is a broad plan for national development where we have the co-operation of all industry.
During the previous administration we placed an official of the Department of Trade and Commerce in the industrial development bank of Canada to try and make the necessary funds available for industrial development. This had a signal success. In round figures it was possible to make available to industries and small businesses just about four times as much money per year as they ever had before. Therefore I think the credit supply is of prime importance. But again, I am against the idea of the government setting up its own credit supply. I would far rather it made the money available to the industrial bank, as in the past, and by working through a board under the direction of the minister this would provide something of an advisory and not a dictatorial nature.
The biggest barrier to full employment is trade, and in this connection I wish to refer to the Gordon report. I do not often refer to it, but at page 60 it says:
In any case, the benefits to be expected from freer trade are impossible to quantify exactly. They may seem to be reckoned only in pennies, whereas the gains to be had from a successful full employment policy or from rapid technological advance may seem to be reckoned in pounds.
That is a little contradictory, of course; but what he is trying to get at is that it is much better to develop efficient production at home than it is to worry about trying to find freer trade policies abroad. In addition, if we are able to produce better products in Canada, and sell them at world market prices, we will establish full employment without asking trade concessions of any kind. And looking at our position at the moment as that of a young nation hitherto engaged in primary industry, and now putting its neck out into manufacturing industry, we cannot expect industrial Europe or the United States to give us the red carpet treatment. They certainly will not if we go into anything like government subsidies for exports.
I think we have already gone too far with government subsidies for exports in many cases, and the emphasis in this new department, if it is set up, should definitely be placed on efficiency. That efficiency can best come by individual, free enterprise, and not by setting up more crown corporations which

are expensive and unfair to private enterprise. This party, for one, firmly stands behind free enterprise.
In connection with exploration I would like to suggest to the government that much can be done in the way of exploration, even in the Northwest Territories and areas above the Arctic circle. It is high time we set up a full geodetic and mineral survey of all our resources to find out exactly what we have. I suggest there are a good many jobs to be provided by this exploration, and surely it would be better to hire a few thousand men to find out where our roads and railroads to the north should go in order to reach the rich deposits, instead of wasting thousands of miles of roads and rails to reach inferior beds of ore and other natural resources.
I suggest something could also be done in the tax atmosphere. The proposed department should consult freely with the Department of National Revenue to see if something can be done taxwise to encourage enterpreneurs to go into research and development of our own resources. The Department of National Defence might well be consulted. Sometimes we lose sight of the fact that many things like oil and steel are just as important to defence as to anything else, especially when they are turned into fuel for tanks or shells for guns. It might be that the people in charge of defence would recommend more efficient networks of roads and railways to service supplies in time of disruption and war.
I wish to refer once more to the royal commission on Canada's economic prospects, at page 62:
There will be a temptation to forget that what is being tested is no less than the vigour and resiliency of free societies and that, in such times, the continuance of comparatively inefficient production may be an expensive luxury.
Surely the men who wrote this book and who occupy the treasury benches cannot repudiate this; therefore I would expect them to lean away from socialism. It is the resilience of our modern free society on the North American continent which is under test. I think before we go ahead with this type of planning we should make up our minds on that big question: are we socialists, or are we not? If we are socialists, this kind of planning is going to end up in economic dictatorship, and that would be fatal to our way of life. If this department, when it is set up, is to preserve free enterprise, I think we had better take a good look at this act and make sure that we do not give dictatorial powers to the proposed minister.

Mr. Speaker, coming from a constituency where industry plays a very important part, I cannot miss this opportunity to say a few words about the measure under consideration.
Of course, like all other members of the house, I am deeply concerned to see that our industry and trade keep on developing and any measure or effort that would increase production and, consequently, trade, cannot but be supported without question by one and all.
However, according to some members on the other side of the house who have taken part in the debate, it seems that we should, on this side, adopt all the measures presented, without asking questions and without studying them thoroughly.
Mr. Speaker, you will agree with me that what we heard during the days that immediately followed the budget speech amply warrant our asking questions before giving our support to the different measures which are submitted to us. It would seem that the present government have not given enough consideration to many of the pieces of legislation which they introduce in the house.


I should like to make a few remarks about the statements of both the hon. member for Essex West (Mr. Gray) and the hon. member for Toronto-Broadview (Mr. Hahn). Both said that before introducing this measure, the government should have made sure that there was a need for it. That is what I am asking myself, Mr. Speaker. Is it really necessary to set up a department to increase our trade and to stimulate industry in Canada?
To hear my hon. friends speak, you would think that under the previous government there was general stagnation in this country and that our trade was on the brink of bankruptcy, that it was going down instead of increasing.
However, Mr. Speaker, looking at the figures, we note that under the former Conservative government, foreign trade as well as domestic trade have constantly increased. And to clear up any apprehension or any doubt in the minds of my friends opposite, I will put on Hansard a few figures illustrating the rate of development of our trade under the administration of Right Hon. John Diefenbaker's Conservative government.
The figures that I shall quote, Mr. Speaker, are from the December 29, 1962 edition of the review entitled The Economist. We can see from those figures that the rate of economic growth has been higher in Canada, in 1962, than in any other country, and the following comparison proves that what I have just said is true. In Canada, the increase has been 8 per cent while in Italy, it was 6.3 per cent; in the United States, it was 5 per cent; in Japan, 4.5 per cent; in Sweden and in Norway, 4 per cent; in Germany, 3.6 per cent; in Belgium, 3.2 per cent; in the Netherlands, 2.5 per cent and in Great Britain, 1 per cent.
All of which goes to show beyond any doubt, Mr. Speaker, that when our friends opposite claim we were leading trade and business in this country to bankruptcy, that is absolutely false.
When one looks at the advance made by the whole Canadian production since 1957, one finds that it has increased by 26.6 per cent. Canadian production, which in 1957 stood at $31.9 billion, had risen in 1962 to $40.4 billion.
As for our exports, Mr. Speaker, for the months of January to October 1957, they amounted to $4,006 million, while for the same period in 1962, they had reached $5,240 million, an increase of 30.8 per cent.

That, Mr. Speaker, certainly had its effect on the labour market because, during the years mentioned, that is from 1957 to 1962, there were half a million more workers than at the time we took office, in 1957.
If this government wants to take measures to encourage further our trade, very well. But I believe that the measure now before us will lead especially to the setting up of a team of technicians and employees of all types, with the result that more importance, more influence and more control will be given to bureaucracy.
I think that we should stop a minute and take a good look at this measure. As for me, I am prepared to co-operate as much as possible so that our workers in the plants, which is our first step towards trade, can have an even more regular work week, based on a greater production.
I am of the opinion that it would be appropriate, if the present government wants to increase our foreign trade in particular, to continue the practice started by the minister of trade and commerce who preceded the one now in charge of that department.
You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that we sent to foreign countries trade missions whose excellent work resulted in a great number of orders for our Canadian industrialists. I feel we should study that possibility further in order to extend that service we had already started.
I will probably have other remarks to make when the measure is to be given further consideration, but for the moment, like my hon. friend from Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon) I wish to point out that the recent measure imposing an 11 per cent tax on construction materials, is liable to hurt greatly the development of our trade. I think I should not miss the opportunity to urge the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) to help his colleague the proposed minister of industry, by removing as soon as possible this tax which will result in unemployment and a higher cost of living.
The present department has a staff with the required qualifications to serve the nation efficiently, especially that sector of our national economy. In my opinion, if we call upon people who have neither the practical experience nor the know-how of our present civil servants who have been working in this field for a large part of their lives, we not only make a mistake, but perhaps also deprive ourselves of the knowledge and experience

speechtext:
We are dealing tonight in this house with an important matter-the creation of a new department of government. Sometimes my memory, going back more years than I like to recall, reminds me of something I learned as a school boy about the burial of Sir John Moore:
We buried him darkly at dead of night,
The sods with our bayonets turning.
I am wondering if we are not burying the Department of Trade and Commerce, "the sods with our bayonets turning", without our having a much closer look at the obsequies of this department. I do not think we should allow the department to sink into oblivion over the realm of forgetfulness, without discussing the matter for just a moment or two.
I was particularly interested in this matter, Mr. Speaker, and this afternoon I did some checking into the creation of various departments. I do not know the historical background to this-the Secretary of State (Mr. Pickersgill) has a knowledge of history even greater than mine-but I think when you read through the authorities respecting the ministers of the various departments, the only fact of this character to which you will find reference is the fact that the minister of trade and commerce is to be a member of Her Majesty's privy council. Apparently no other minister, Mr. Speaker, was entitled to that prerogative when that department was first created. I presume this is an inheritance from the year 1867, and we have had some overriding legislation dealing with this in the meantime. But I think the Secretary of State, whose knowledge of history, as I say, is even greater than mine, will be rather intrigued when he looks back through the departments and finds that the minister of trade and commerce shall be a member of Her Majesty's Privy Council.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the reference of the Secretary of State. But in any event, whether the minister minimizes it or not, I suggest to the house leader, through you, sir, that this legislation which is before us tonight does minimize, and minimize substantially, the area, shall I say the prerogative, which heretofore had been occupied by the minister and the Department of Trade and Commerce. When I say that I am not reflecting in any way at all upon the minister, who I understand from press references and in moving the bill this afternoon would, if parliament sees fit to pass this legislation, become minister of the new department of industry. I can pay my tribute to him. Going back over a good many years, when I was not even a member of the House of Commons, I came to him when he was a deputy minister of a department, and may I say that he was an exceptionally able deputy. I have never forgotten the good advice, suggestions, consultations and conferences which we had. If it is necessary to have a department of industry presided over by a minister, I am quite sure that the man who has been suggested, in other words the Minister of Defence Production (Mr. Drury), could not be bettered. If the proposed minister, the present Minister of Defence Production, and I could sit down in the secret conclaves of my room over a glass of lemon juice, or something of that kind, where we could discuss the organization of this department, my guess is that he would be the first to suggest that there should not be the bifurcation which is now taking place within the department.

At this early hour of the evening, Mr. Speaker, I do not know how the hon. gentleman from Newfoundland, whose mind naturally goes to concoctions to which we in Nova Scotia are not addicted, could even think of Lemon Hart; but if he has that in mind, far be it for me to disillusion him, because it is only three minutes to


ten and I am sure he would be able to clarify his mind on that situation.
However, I really have a tremendous sympathy for the present Minister of Defence Production under this bill, which we will be discussing further, depending upon the agreements reached between the house leaders, I presume tomorrow morning. All of us in this house remember the way in which he stood up in his place a few days ago, having come back from Washington and told us of the problems with which he had been confronted, how he hoped that we could engage in more sales of defence mechanisms to the United States, how we had to accommodate the Americans by buying more from them. But we were assured by the minister in charge of defence production that there was a reasonable chance that Canada might engage in selling proportionately as much to the Americans; that we might maintain an uneasy balance in view of the balance of payments problems.
Now, in addition to that, the hon. gentleman, who is obviously overworked in trying to accomplish that end, has to concern himself with something about area development, whatever that may mean-and in that matter I would refer him to the way the provinces have dealt with this problem. And then he has to deal with the overriding problem of developing the industrial life of this country. I have heard of superman, but certainly the Minister of Defence Production, if the press reports are right and if he has to deal with these problems with which I have suggested he may be confronted, deserves the prayers and best wishes of all members of the House of Commons.
With that, Mr. Speaker, may I call it ten o'clock?

I would be very happy to. I have conferred with hon. gentlemen opposite and I think there is a general disposition to accept a suggestion that was made in fact last Friday, I think by the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings, that perhaps we

might all benefit by celebrating the 1st of July in some place else than here. I believe there is agreement, which could be recorded and therefore be an order of the house, that we should take the supply motion on Tuesday and Wednesday of next week, instead of on Monday and Tuesday; that it would be understood that if there is an amendment and a subamendment, the vote would come at 9.30 on Tuesday. If there is only an amendment and no subamendment, the vote would come at 9.45, so that the time left on Wednesday would be available for general grievances. The vote on the main motion would then come at a quarter to six on Wednesday. If there is general agreement in the house to that effect, then I think it might be so ordered.
